meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Reorganizing is a Wonderful Method for Creating the Illusion of Progress while Actually Producing Confusion, Inefficiency, and Demoralization'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Petronius. Charlton Ogburn Jr. wrote it in Harper's Magazine, January 1957, recalling Merrill's Marauders; a Petronius credit appears by 1966.

answer.label: Not Gaius Petronius Arbiter — actually Charlton Ogburn Jr.
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Ogburn’s article “Merrill’s Marauders: The Truth about an Incredible Adventure” in Harper’s Magazine, January 1957, where he recalled his unit being reorganized again and again during training. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that Petronius ever wrote it. The popular wording is a simplified version of Ogburn’s sentence, and the Petronius credit had appeared by 1966.

source.heading: The original passage

docMeta.dd: Merrill’s Marauders: The Truth about an Incredible Adventure
Harper’s Magazine, January 1957 (vol. 214, no. 1280; quote on pp. 32–33, per Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt: We trained hard, but it seemed that every time we were beginning to form up into teams we would be reorganized. Presumably the plans for our employment were being changed. I was to learn later in life that, perhaps because we are so good at organizing, we tend as a nation to meet any new situation by reorganizing; and a wonderful method it can be for creating the illusion of progress while producing confusion, inefficiency, and demoralization. During our reorganizations, several commanding officers were tried out on us, which added to the discontinuity.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence that Gaius Petronius Arbiter employed this quotation” and credits it to Charlton Ogburn Jr., in Harper’s Magazine (January 1957) and his book The Marauders (1959).
Wikiquote’s Petronius page ↗ lists the passage under “Misattributed” and credits Charlton Ogburn’s “Merrill’s Marauders” in Harper’s Magazine, January 1957.
Harper’s own archive ↗ lists the January 1957 article “Merrill’s Marauders” by Charlton Ogburn, subtitled “The truth about an incredible adventure.”
Wikipedia’s Ogburn article ↗ says the quote is often misattributed to Petronius and points to D. S. Brown’s note “Petronius or Ogburn” in Public Administration Review.
source.excerptNote: Passage as transcribed by Quote Investigator, which verified it on microfilm. The popular “Reorganizing is a wonderful method…” form doesn’t appear in this text. It is a shortened version of the middle sentence.

author.name: Charlton Ogburn Jr.
author.heading: About the real author
author.metaLine: 1911–1998 · American writer, Merrill’s Marauders communications officer
author.bio: Born in Atlanta, Ogburn served in the China Burma India Theater in World War II as a communications officer with Merrill’s Marauders. His 1957 Harper’s article about the unit led to his 1959 book The Marauders, which was filmed as Merrill’s Marauders (1962). He later became a leading Oxfordian, best known for The Mysterious William Shakespeare (1984).

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on a Roman
misattribution.intro: Ogburn’s 1957 complaint about Army reorganizations got passed around without his name. Later it was dressed up as ancient wisdom.

items.why: Petronius was a courtier of Nero and the likely author of the Satyricon. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that he wrote the line. The person who sent QI the question couldn’t find it in any ancient work either.

items.who: “One of the officers of Merrill’s Marauders”
items.why: Col. George H. Hollingsworth quoted a slightly modified version of the Harper’s text and credited it only to an unnamed Marauders officer, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Rep. John P. Saylor, quoting “Petronius Arbiter”
items.why: In a September 1966 article about overlapping federal agencies, Saylor credited the line to “Petronius Arbiter, a Roman official at the time of Nero.” Quote Investigator writes that “by 1966 the statement had been reassigned” to Petronius (QI ↗).
Townsend, who had led Avis, printed the quotation in his “Reorganizing” section with a Petronius credit. The reader who asked QI says a footnote dated it “circa A.D. 60” (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Credit it to Charlton Ogburn Jr., Harper’s Magazine, January 1957, which he later reworded in The Marauders (1959). That is the conclusion of Quote Investigator ↗, and Wikiquote ↗ agrees.

context.heading: Why the line endures
lead: Ogburn was remembering training with Merrill’s Marauders in World War II. Every time his men started to form up into teams, the unit was reorganized again, and commanding officers kept changing. He turned that experience into a broader point about how institutions react to anything new.

His 1959 book The Marauders reworded the passage: Americans “have a gift for organizing,” and reorganizing creates “the illusion of progress at a mere cost of confusion, inefficiency and demoralization” (as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗). Management writers later picked up the shorter form. Crediting it to an ancient Roman made the joke feel timeless, but the observation comes from a 20th-century American soldier.
